en: A certain Yakṣa, whose greatness had been eclipsed by his lord’s curse— for which he was heavy with remorse due to separation from his beloved and who had been negligent in his duty—
took up residence in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, where the waters were sanctified by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter and the trees offered cool shade.
On that mountain, having spent several months separated from his beloved, that lover— his forearms scarred by the slipping of his golden bracelets—
beheld on the first day of the month of Āṣāḍha a cloud embracing the peaks, as beautiful to behold as an elephant returning from sporting in a mud bank.
Standing somehow before him for the sake of supporting the *ketaka* flower, the attendant of the King of Kings brooded for a long time with tears within;
for at the sight of a cloud, the mind of even a happy man undergoes a change—how much more so when the person longing for a neck-embrace is situated far away?
When the rainy season was near, he, seeking a means to sustain the life of his beloved, intended to send news consisting of his own welfare by means of a cloud;
to that cloud, for whom he had prepared an offering of fresh *kuṭaja* flowers, he joyfully uttered words of welcome preceded by expressions of affection.
"Where is a cloud—a mere conjunction of smoke, light, water, and wind—and where are the meanings of a message, which must be delivered by living beings with functional senses?
Thus, disregarding these considerations out of eagerness, the Guhyaka made his request; for those afflicted by love become wretched in their supplications toward both sentient and insentient things.
I know you to be the primal spirit of Indra, capable of assuming any form at will, born into the world-renowned lineage of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds.
Therefore, though my kinsmen are far away, I have come to you as a suppliant by the power of fate; for a request made to one of superior merit is better than one granted to a base person.
O cloud, you are the refuge for those who are tormented; therefore, carry my message to my beloved, who has been separated from me by the wrath of the Lord of Wealth.
You must go to her dwelling named Alakā, where the palaces are washed by the moonlight from the head of Hara as he stands in the outer garden.
As you ascend the path of the wind, the wives of travelers, lifting up the ends of their tresses and finding comfort through trust, will gaze upon you.
For who, when you are thus equipped for departure, would neglect a wife distressed by separation—unless, like me, he were a person whose livelihood depends on another?

Take leave of this lofty mountain, your dear friend, embracing him whose slopes are marked by the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus—those revered by men. For from time to time, upon meeting you, he manifests his affection by shedding warm tears born of long separation.
A favorable breeze gently fans you, and this sweet-voiced cātaka bird, longing for water, warbles on your left;
surely the cranes, their bonds strengthened by the stability of the rainy season's conception and forming long lines, will serve you in the sky, so pleasing to the eye.
And you, whose path is unimpeded, will surely see that wife of your brother, who is intent on counting the days and remains faithful and uninjured;
for in separation, the bond of hope generally restrains the flower-like heart of women, which is otherwise prone to immediate collapse.

And having heard your thunder, so pleasing to the ear and capable of making the earth rich with sprouting mushrooms, the royal swans, longing for Lake Mānasa, will become your companions in the sky as far as Kailāsa, carrying bits of lotus stalks as provisions for the journey. (KMdV 12)
First, O cloud, hear the path as I describe it, which is favorable for your journey; thereafter you shall hear my message, a drink for the ears.
You will proceed by placing your footstep upon mountain peaks whenever you are weary, and you shall travel having repeatedly consumed the light waters of the streams when they are exhausted.

"Is the wind carrying away the peak of the mountain?"—thus watched with wide-eyed wonder by the innocent wives of the Siddhas looking upwards, take flight from this place of succulent Nicula trees toward the north, avoiding the lapping of the thick trunks of the world-elephants on your path through the sky. (KMdV 14)
This fragment of Indra’s bow, appearing before you like a mingling of jewel-reflections, emerges from the top of an anthill;
with it, your dark body will attain an exceeding luster, like that of Viṣṇu in his cowherd guise when adorned with a peacock feather of shimmering radiance.

Drunk in by the eyes of the village women—eyes moist with affection and ignorant of the play of the brow, for they believe the fruit of agriculture depends entirely upon you—ascend the Māla field, fragrant from the recent turning of the plow; then, having turned your course slightly to the west, proceed once more toward the north.
Mount Āmrakūṭa will properly bear you upon its summit—exhausted by the fatigue of the journey and having quenched the forest fires with its showers—as one does a guest;
for even a lowly person does not turn his back on a friend who has arrived seeking refuge out of regard for past favors, much less one so exalted as he.

When you, who possess the hue of a glossy braid of hair, have ascended to the peak, the mountain—its slopes covered by mango trees radiant with ripened fruit—will surely attain a state worthy of being gazed upon by celestial couples: dark in its center like the breast of the Earth, and pale in its remaining expanse.
Having stayed for a moment in that bower enjoyed by the wives of forest-dwellers, you— your pace now greatly quickened by the discharge of water—
will cross the further path and behold the Revā river at the rugged, rocky foot of the Vindhya mountains, scattered as if it were the decorative patterns painted upon the body of an elephant.
Having shed your rain, you should proceed taking up that water which is scented by the bitter ichor of wild elephants and whose flow is checked by groves of rose-apple trees;
O cloud, the wind will not be able to shake you, for you possess internal substance. Indeed, everything empty becomes light, while fullness leads to weightiness.
Seeing the *nīpa* tree greenish-brown with its half-grown filaments, and the *kandalī* plants along the marshy banks putting forth their first buds;
and smelling the fragrance of the earth, which becomes even more sweet in burnt forests, those deer will indicate the path for you as the clouds release drops of water.
I foresee, my friend, that even though you wish to depart quickly for the sake of my beloved, there will be delay at every mountain fragrant with *kakubha* flowers;
for you will be greeted by peacocks who, with tears in their eyes and white-cornered glances, offer a welcome through their cries—therefore, you must somehow resolve to proceed swiftly.
With the enclosures of their groves pale in hue from *ketaka* flowers split open by their needle-like thorns, with village shrines crowded by the nest-building of domestic pigeons,
and with the edges of their rose-apple forests darkened by the ripening of fruit, the Daśārṇa country will, upon your arrival, become a place where swans remain for only a few days.
Having gone to their capital city, renowned by the name Vidiśā, situated in those directions, you shall immediately obtain the full fruit of your amorous desires;
there you will drink the sweet water of the Vetravatī river, which, sounding pleasantly from its banks, has waves that move like a face with a frown.
There you should dwell upon the mountain named Nīcairghaṇṭa for the sake of rest; it seems to thrill with joy at the touch of your presence through its *kadamba* trees in full bloom.
There, by means of its stone grottoes exhaling the fragrances of the amorous dalliances of courtesans, it proclaims the unrestrained youthfulness of the city-dwellers.
Having rested, you shall sprinkle with fresh droplets of water the buds of the *yūthikā* jasmine in the gardens growing on the banks of the forest rivers;

and by providing shade, you will become momentarily acquainted with the faces of the flower-gathering maidens, whose ear-lotuses have grown weary from the pain of removing the sweat upon their cheeks.
Although the path you have set out upon toward the northern quarter is circuitous, do not be averse to the embrace of Ujjayinī’s palatial mansions;
for if you do not take delight there in the eyes of the city women—trembling with flashes of lightning and darting with restless glances—you will have been utterly deceived.

On the way, O friend, become an insider to the waters of the Nirvindhyā river as she flows along—she whose girdle-string is the rows of birds warbling amidst the agitation of her waves, who moves with a charming faltering, and reveals the whorls of her navel; for in the presence of lovers, the first word of affection from women is indeed a playful coquetry.

O fortunate one, having crossed that Sindhu river—whose meager waters have become like a single braid of hair, whose banks possess a pale luster due to the withered leaves falling from the trees growing upon them, and which reveals your beauty through its state of separation—you must provide that very means by which she may abandon her emaciation. (KMdV 29)
Having reached Avanti, where the village elders are experts in the tales of Udayana, follow the previously mentioned city of Viśālā, which is vast in its splendor;

it is like a radiant fragment of heaven brought down to earth by the remaining merits of those celestial beings who have gone to the world of mortals once the fruits of their good deeds had diminished.
There, at dawn, the breeze from the Siprā— prolonging the sharp, sweetly-intoxicated warbling of the cranes, fragrant with its friendship for the scent of blooming lotuses,
and pleasing to the limbs of women— removes their exhaustion from lovemaking, like a beloved lover offering flattering words of entreaty.

Having spent the night in her palaces— fragrant with flowers and marked by the red lac from the feet of lovely women— he, whose inner soul was weary from the journey, his body refreshed by the smoke from hair-adorning incense wafting through the lattice windows, and receiving offerings of dance from the household peacocks out of affection for their kin, [proceeded].
Beheld with reverence by the Gaṇas as possessing the hue of your master’s neck, you shall go to the holy abode of Caṇḍeśvara, the preceptor of the three worlds—

a place where the gardens are shaken by breezes from the Gandhavatī river, fragrant with the pollen of blue water-lilies and scented by the musk-like aroma of young women engaged in sporting in its waters.
O cloud, even if you must wait for another time, you should remain until the sun comes within the range of your vision at Mahākāla;
there, by serving as the praiseworthy drum for the evening offerings of the Trident-bearer, you will obtain the full fruit of your deep-thundering roars.
There, the courtesans— their girdles tinkling at every step as they move about with playful grace, their hands weary from waving fly-whisks whose handles are encrusted with the luster of jewels—
shall, upon receiving from you the first drops of rain that bring pleasure to their nail-marks, cast at you side-long glances as long as a swarm of bees.
Afterwards, having merged into the circle of the forest of tall *bhujaga* trees and bearing the evening glow as red as a fresh *japā* flower,
satisfy the desire of Pāśupati for the moist elephant-hide at the commencement of his dance, while Bhavānī’s eyes remain motionless, their agitation stilled, as she gazes upon you with devotion.

As women travel there at night toward their lovers' dwellings along the royal highway, where the light is blocked by darkness so thick it could be pierced by a needle, show them the path with the lightning—
glossy as a streak of gold upon a touchstone— but do not be loud with the thundering of rain-showers, for they are timid.

Having spent that night on some palace balcony where the pigeons are asleep, you—whose consort, the lightning, is weary from long play—should once again traverse the remainder of the journey when the sun is seen; for friends who have undertaken a task for their friend do not indeed delay.
At that time, lovers must pacify the tears of their jilted wives; therefore, quickly leave the path of the sun.
For he too has returned to wipe away the dew-tears from the lotus-face of the night-lily, and if you obstruct his rays, he will feel no small resentment toward you.
When the waters of the deep river are as clear as the mind, even the reflection of your own self—naturally beautiful—will find entry therein.
Therefore, you ought not, out of stubbornness, to render fruitless her glances, white as lilies, which are like the darting leaps of shimmering minnows.

Having stolen her blue garment of water, which has slipped from its hips of the riverbanks and reached the branches of the reeds as if held by her hand, your departure, my friend, will somehow be difficult while you hang over it; for who, having tasted its sweetness, is able to abandon a woman whose thighs are the sandbanks?
A cool breeze— holy from its contact with the fragrance of the earth revived by your own radiance, being drunk in by elephants with a pleasant sound echoing through the openings of their trunks,
and ripening the wild figs of the forest— will blow softly as you approach the mountain that precedes the gods.
There, transforming yourself into a cloud of flowers, may you bathe Skanda—who has made his dwelling there—with showers of blossoms moistened by the waters of the celestial Ganges;
for that splendor, which surpasses the sun and was gathered from the mouth of the fire for the sake of protecting Indra’s armies, resides within him as the bearer of the new moon.

Afterwards, you should cause that peacock of Pāvaka to dance with your roars, which are deepened by the resonance of the mountain— [the peacock] whose fallen tail-feather, encircled by streaks of light, Bhavānī places upon her ear out of affection for her son, reaching as far as her blue lotus-like ear, its outer corner washed by the luster of Hara’s moon.

Having thus worshipped the god born in the forest of Śara, and having traversed the path whose way was cleared by pairs of lute-bearing Siddhas fearing the spray of water-drops, you should descend [to the Narmadā],
honoring the fame of Rantideva which sprang from the sacrifice of cows and which has been transformed on earth into the form of a river.

When you, the thief of the peacock’s plumage, bend down to take water from her, the travelers in the sky will gaze with eyes cast far down upon that river’s current— which, though broad, appears slender due to its distance— seeing it like a single string of pearls from the earth, with a large sapphire at its center.

Having crossed that river, proceed, making your own form the object of the curious glances of the women of Daśapura— glances whose playful movements are familiar with the arching of creeper-like brows, which reveal the shimmering dark and variegated luster of their eyes as they lift their lashes, and which steal the beauty of bees following the scattering of *kunda* flowers.
Descending with your shadow upon the land of Brahmāvarta, you should resort to that Kuru field which betokens the great battle of the kṣatriyas—
a place where the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow showered the faces of the kings with hundreds of sharp arrows, just as you rain down upon lotuses with your torrents of water.

O gentle one, after visiting those waters of the Sarasvatī which the wielder of the plow (Balarāma)— having abandoned the wine of his beloved Revatī, whose eyes were marked by beauty, and having turned away from battle out of affection for his kinsmen— resorted to, you too shall become clear within, remaining black only in outward appearance.
Therefore, you should go to the daughter of Jahnu, who descended from the king of mountains at Anukanakhala; she is a flight of stairs to heaven for the sons of Sagara.
She, as if laughing with her foam at the knitting of the eyebrows on Gaurī’s face, seized Śambhu by the hair with her wave-hands clinging to the moon.
If you, hanging from the sky by your forequarters like the celestial elephant Airāvata, were to look askance at her water, which is as clear as pure crystal, while intending to drink,
she would become delightful through your shadow suddenly gliding upon her stream— a union with the Yamunā occurring in an unexpected place.
Having reached that very mountain, the source of that river, whose rocks are perfumed by the musk from the navels of deer and which is white with snow,
you shall sit upon its peak to dispel the fatigue of the journey and display a lovely splendor comparable to the mud dug up by the bull of the Three-Eyed God.

If, as the wind blows, a forest fire born from the friction of the trunks of *sarala* trees should afflict you—extinguishing the bushy tails of yaks with its sparks—you ought to quench it with thousands of streams of water; for the wealth of the noble has as its fruit the alleviation of the suffering of those in distress.

But those śarabhas who, unable to endure your roar, shall out of arrogant pride attempt to leap over you—the one who is unassailable—in order to break your body, you should scatter them with a laugh-like shower of tumultuous hailstones; for who indeed does not become an object of contempt when their efforts are directed toward a fruitless undertaking?
There, bowing with devotion, you should circumambulate the clearly visible footprint of the moon-crested Lord upon the rock, where offerings are perpetually presented by the Siddhas;
for upon seeing it, those who possess faith, their sins shaken off, become fit to attain his eternal station among the Gaṇas after the departure of the senses.
The hollow bamboos, being filled by the winds, resound sweetly; and the victory over Tripura is sung by the Kinnara women with impassioned voices.
If your own sound should resound like a drum within the caves, then indeed the entire purpose of the musical performance of Paśupati would be realized there.

Having passed beyond those various wonders on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain, you should proceed toward the northern direction through the Krauñca-cleft— that gateway for the swans and the path to the glory of Bhṛgupati— which, with its oblique expanse, is as beautiful as the dark foot of Viṣṇu when he was intent upon subduing Bali.
And having gone upward, may you become a guest of Kailāsa, whose mountain ridges were uplifted by the arms of the Ten-faced one and who serves as a mirror for the celestial women;
a mountain that stands expanding the sky with its lily-white peaks, appearing like the accumulated, nightly loud laughter of the Three-eyed Lord.
I foresee that when you, resembling smooth crushed collyrium, stand upon its slope, the playful beauty of that mountain— now as white as the freshly severed tusk of an elephant—
will become a sight to be gazed upon with steady eyes, like a dark garment draped over the shoulder of the wielder of the plow.
And if Gaurī, having cast off her blue serpent-bracelet and with a hand offered by Śambhu, should wander on foot upon the pleasure-mountain, then you—
your body formed of the art of waves and with the water within you solidified— become a staircase for her, providing a pleasant touch to her feet during her ascents.

There, the celestial maidens will surely lead you into the state of a fountain-house by making you enter within and emit sprays of water. O friend, if you do not wish to be released from them once you have been caught in the heat, you must frighten those girls, who are fond of play, with thunders harsh to the ear.
Taking from Lake Mānasa water that brings forth golden lotuses, and at will providing for a moment the pleasure of a face-veil to Airāvaṇa,
you should enter that mountain— clear as crystal and distinguished by its shadows— shaking the garments of the Kalpa-trees with breezes laden with droplets of water.
O wanderer at will, having seen Alakā upon his lap—like a lover whose silken garment is the Ganges slipping down—you shall not fail to recognize it;
there, the lofty celestial chariots carry a mass of clouds that, like a passionate woman, bears aloft a cluster of pearls woven into her curls, while emitting a spray of water at the proper season.

There, palaces with their various special qualities are able to rival you: they possess lightning in the form of lovely women; they bear rainbows in the form of variegated paintings; they have the sound of drums beaten for music; they have a smooth, deep resonance; they contain water within; they have floors made of jewels; they are lofty; and their peaks touch the clouds.

Where the young women hold a play-lotus in their hands, have braided their hair with young *kunda* flowers, and have brought a pallor to the beauty of their faces with the pollen of *rodhra* blossoms;
where they wear fresh *kurabaka* at their tresses, lovely *śirīṣa* at their ears, and *nīpa* flowers at the parting of their hair, produced by your arrival.
In that city, the Yakṣas, accompanied by their most excellent women, resort to palace terraces made of white jewels, which are adorned with the reflections of stars as if they were flowers;
there, while your deep-toned drums are slowly struck, they enjoy the honey produced by the wish-fulfilling trees, which has pleasure as its fruit.

There, the moonstones—suspended from webs of thread and dripping with clear drops of water—dispel the physical exhaustion born of lovemaking in women who have been revived by the embraces of their beloveds; they do so as they are uplifted by the rays of the moon, which become bright upon the cessation of your obstruction.
Where clouds like you, led by the wind to the upper terraces of the palaces, instantly cause damage to the paintings with their fresh raindrops,
then— seized by apprehension as it were— they emerge through the lattices, shattered and skillfully imitating columns of smoke.
Where, when their lovers impulsively snatch away with unsteady hands the garments of the Yakṣa women— garments loosened by the slipping of the waist-knot—
the handfuls of scented powder thrown by those women, bewildered by shame, become fruitless efforts even as they reach the jewel-lamps that stand tall before them.

There, at the rising of the sun, the nocturnal path of amorous women is indicated by *mandāra* flowers fallen from their tresses as they hurried along, by golden lotuses slipped from their ears and fashioned as ornaments, and by necklaces whose threads have snapped, their pearls clinging to the fragrance of their breasts.
Knowing that the God who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth dwells there in person, the God of Love generally does not carry his bow out of fear;

for him, the task is accomplished solely by the graceful movements of beautiful women, which are unfailing against the targets of lovers, with their eyes cast forth along with the knitting of their brows.
There, to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth, our home is visible from afar by its gateway, beautiful as the bow of the gods;
near it stands a young mandāra tree, nurtured by my beloved like a foster-son, which bends low with clusters of blossoms reachable by the hand.
And in this place there is a pond with a flight of steps bound in emerald stone, strewn with golden lotus buds on glossy stalks of beryl;
the swans dwelling in its waters, their sorrows dispelled, will not long for Lake Mānasa even upon seeing you, for it is so close at hand.

O friend, on whose bank stands a pleasure-mound with its peak covered by exquisite sapphires, beautiful to behold with its enclosure of golden plantain trees— seeing you with lightning flashing at your edge, my heart, distressed and thinking "this is dear to my wife," remembers that very place.
Here, near the mādhavī bower surrounded by a hedge of *kuravaka* shrubs, stand the lovely red *aśoka* with its trembling new shoots and the *kesara*;
one longs for your friend’s left foot along with me, while the other, under the pretext of a ritual requirement (*dohada*), craves the wine from her mouth.

And in its center stands a golden pillar with a crystal slab, bound at its base with jewels that have the luster of young bamboo; upon it, at the close of day, your friend the peacock perches, made to dance by my beloved with cymbals made charming by her tinkling bracelets. KMdV_76 //
O virtuous one, by these characteristics impressed upon your heart, and having seen Śaṅkha and Padma with their forms painted near the doorway, you must recognize [the house].
Indeed, due to my separation, this dwelling now possesses a dim luster; for surely, in the absence of the sun, a lotus does not maintain its own natural splendor.
Having immediately assumed the small body of a young elephant for the sake of a swift descent, you should sit upon the lovely peak of the pleasure-mountain previously mentioned;
there, you ought to make the flash of lightning—falling into the interior of the house—appear as a faint glimmer, resembling the flickering of a swarm of fireflies.

Slender, dark-complexioned, with teeth like mountain peaks and lips like ripe bimba fruit, thin-waisted, with the glance of a startled doe and a deep-set navel; moving slowly from the weight of her hips and slightly bent by her breasts—she who might be there would be as if the Creator’s very first creation among the realm of young women. (KMdV 79)
You should know her to be one of few words, my very second life, like a solitary female ruddy goose when I, her mate, have gone far away;
as these days pass, heavy with intense longing, I think that young girl has become transformed in appearance, like a lotus plant withered by the cold.
Surely her face— its eyes swollen from intense weeping, its lower lip discolored by the heat of many sighs,
resting upon her hand, and its features only partially discernible due to hanging tresses— bears the wretchedness of the moon whose luster is marred when obscured by your approach.
She will soon fall within your sight—either distracted by her ritual offerings, or painting a likeness of me emaciated by separation as she contemplates its inner meaning;
or perhaps asking the sweet-voiced śārikā bird in its cage, "O silent one, do you remember your master? For you were indeed his beloved."
Or perhaps, O gentle one, having placed the lute upon her lap covered by a soiled garment, she desires to sing a song composed of verses marked with my name;
yet, somehow managing to tune the strings which have been dampened by her tears, she repeatedly forgets even the musical modulations (mūrcchanā) she herself has fashioned.
Either counting the remaining months of the period beginning on the day of departure by placing flowers on the threshold,
or savoring the union that has begun within her heart— these, generally speaking, are the diversions of women during separation from their lovers.

On the first day of our separation, she tied her hair into a single braid, casting aside her flower-garland; at the end of the curse, when my grief has dissolved, that same braid must be unloosed by me.
She now repeatedly brushes with her hand—its nails untrimmed—that single braid which is rough and uneven, as it has become distressed by his touch, drawing it away from the curve of her cheek.

I fear that separation will not weary your friend as much during the day when she is occupied with tasks, as it will at night when she is devoid of diversion and her grief is more intense; therefore, standing at the window near her bed on the ground, look upon that virtuous woman at midnight while she is awake, and gladden her with my messages.
Emaciated by longing, with one side of her body pressed against the bed of separation—like the slender crescent of the moon remaining at the edge of the eastern horizon;
she longs for sleep, wondering how even a dream-union with me might come to pass, yet finds no room for it as her path is blocked by a flood of tears from her eyes.
She who, with sighs that distress her bud-like lower lip, surely scatters her long, straight locks—rough from her recent bath—down to her cheeks;
she who spent that very night with me as if it were a single moment through the pleasures of her desire, now passes those same nights on beds of separation with hot tears.
With her eyes—cool as the nectar of the moon—entering the path of the lattice-work, she turned toward them out of former affection and then withdrew just as before;
covering them with lashes heavy with tears from exhaustion, she was like a land-lotus on a cloudy day, neither fully blossomed nor asleep.
I know that your friend’s heart is filled with love for me; therefore, in this first separation, I imagine her to be as she is.
It is not that a sense of self-importance makes me so talkative, O fortunate one; rather, my brother, everything I have said will soon be evident to you directly.

Having cast off her ornaments, that frail woman, repeatedly holding her body—already emaciated by grief—upon the lap of the bed, will surely cause even you to shed tears of fresh water; for generally, everyone whose inner soul is moistened becomes moved by compassion.
With the movement of its outer corners obstructed by her curls, devoid of the gloss of collyrium, and having forgotten the play of its eyebrows due to her abstention from wine—
I suspect that as you draw near, the eye of that fawn-eyed maiden, throbbing at the upper lid, will attain the beauty of a blue lotus agitated by the stirring of fish.

Her left thigh—now being released from the marks of my fingernails and, by the turn of fate, forced to abandon its long-familiar string of pearls—will tremble at the end of our union; it is that very limb, as fair as the trunk of a fresh plantain tree, which is accustomed to being massaged by my hands.
O Cloud, at that time, if my beloved should have fallen asleep, sit beside her and endure for just one watch, refraining from thundering;
let there not be a sudden, tight embrace with the coils of her arms slipping from her neck when she somehow finds me, her lover, in a dream.

Having raised her up and comforted her with a breeze cooled by your own spray of water, you should approach that proud woman— who has her eyes fixed upon the window occupied by you and adorned with fresh clusters of jasmine— as she speaks with words like deep thundering.
O lady who has not been widowed, know me to be the beloved friend of your husband, a cloud come into your presence with his messages borne in my heart;
I am he who, with deep and tender sounds, urges on the crowds of weary travelers on the road who long for their wives to loosen their braided hair.

When this has been told, O gentle one, she—looking up at you with a heart swelling with longing, like Maithilī beholding the son of the Wind, and honoring you with her gaze—will listen with rapt attention to what follows; for to women, news of a beloved brought by a friend is but little short of an actual reunion.

The Venerable One would say this to her—both at my request and to do her a kindness: "Your companion, staying at the hermitage on Mount Rāma, is unharmed; he asks after your welfare, O frail one. For living beings for whom misfortune is easily encountered, this alone is what remains to be wished for when separated from loved ones."

With limb against limb—his own slender body pressed against yours, his fevered frame against your burning one, his tearful eyes against your flowing tears; with longing never ceasing against your own longing, and his hot sighs against your even more frequent sighs—he, kept far away by the hostile decree of fate, enters you through his mental constructs alone.

That which you used to whisper eagerly into the ear of your friends before them out of a longing to touch their faces—even that which was expressible by words has now passed beyond the range of hearing and is inaccessible to the eyes; yet, with its words composed out of longing, it speaks this to you through my mouth.

I perceive your limbs in the *śyāmā* creepers, your glances in the eyes of startled does, the shadow of your cheeks in the moon, your tresses in the heavy plumage of peacocks, and the play of your brows in the slender ripples of rivers; alas, O timid one, there is nowhere a single likeness of you existing all together in one place.
Having painted you upon a stone with mineral pigments while feigning anger, I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet;
yet before I can do so, my vision is repeatedly obscured by welling tears—for cruel Fate does not permit our union even in that [portrait].

O virtuous lady, when you have somehow found me in my dreams with my arms outstretched toward the sky for the sake of a merciless embrace, surely the tears of the local deities who behold me fall repeatedly upon the young shoots of the trees— tears as large as pearls.

O virtuous lady, those breezes from the snowy mountains, which immediately burst open the leaf-buds of the *devadāru* trees and proceed toward the south fragrant with the flow of their resin—shall I embrace them, thinking: "If only your body had previously been touched by these"? (KMdV 104)
"How might these nights with their long watches be shortened as if into a single moment? And how might even the day have its heat become faint in every state [of being]?
O lady of tremulous eyes, my heart, for which prayers are difficult to fulfill, has thus been rendered helpless by the intense fevers of the pain of separation from you."
"Indeed, though I reflect much upon myself, I do not find support within my own soul; therefore, O auspicious lady, you too must by no means succumb to despondency.
For whom has absolute happiness ever arrived, or misery exclusively? Conditions rise and fall like the rim of a wheel."
"My curse shall end when the wielder of the Śārṅga bow rises from his serpent-couch; close your eyes for another four months.
Afterwards, we two shall enjoy each of those desires of our own hearts, multiplied by our separation, during nights brightened by the full autumnal moonlight."
Furthermore, he said: "In the past, while you were lying on my bed with your neck entwined around me, you fell asleep and woke up sobbing for some reason;
when I, repeatedly asking, spoke to you with a suppressed laugh, you told me, 'O rogue, I saw you in a dream delighting in the company of someone else.'"
Knowing from this gift of proof that I am well, O dark-eyed one, do not become distrustful of me because of public rumor.
They say that affections diminish somewhat during separation; for those very feelings, through lack of enjoyment, increase in intensity toward the beloved object and become a mass of love.
"O gentle one, have you resolved not to fulfill this service for me? Indeed, I do not doubt your steadfastness;
yet even in silence, you grant water when requested by the *cātaka* birds, for the very act of fulfilling the desired object is the true reply given by the virtuous to those who seek their favor."

Having done this favor for me—who have followed the path of an improper request—whether out of friendship or out of compassion for me as one who is distressed, wander through your desired regions, O cloud, with your beauty enhanced by the rainy season; and may you never, even for a moment, suffer separation from the lightning.
